Based on the retrieved healthcare Q&A matches, a tailored intervention can potentially increase mammography use among HMO (Health Maintenance Organization) women. The most effective approach seems to be telephone counseling, which was found to be particularly effective in promoting change among nonadherent women compared to print materials.

The results suggest that tailored interventions may be preferred over standard or more traditional approaches like printed communications. This is likely because individuals who are nonadherent to mammography screening might require a more personalized and supportive approach to encourage them to schedule appointments.

However, it's also worth noting that additional interventions will be needed to maintain women's adherence to mammography. This highlights the importance of ongoing efforts to improve the effectiveness and reach of tailored interventions in various settings.

It is clear that there are multiple sub-questions related to this topic, such as why tailored print materials may not have been more effective, what specific barriers might be contributing to low mammography use among HMO women, or how tailored interventions can address these issues. Addressing each of these questions explicitly will require further research and data collection.

In conclusion, while the evidence suggests that tailored interventions like telephone counseling are effective in increasing mammography use among HMO women, more work is needed to understand the complexities surrounding this issue and to develop more effective solutions for supporting individual adherence to screening recommendations.
